newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Greenpeace protests at Nestle on soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace protests at Nestle on soybeans.

text.p: Greenpeace demonstrators fighting the use of genetically altered soybeans in food draped a protest banner from Nestle SA's headquarters in Switzerland on Monday before being dispersed by police.
"Gene food: Force fed by Nestle" said the banner spread out by a handful of environmentalist activists who swung from ropes from the roof at the world's largest food company.
Some three dozen activists called on Nestle to distance itself from genetically engineered (GE) soybeans, which they call a risky experiment with nature that could endanger human health.

"Claiming that a separation of GE beans from conventional beans is impossible, American and European multinational companies tried to confront the European consumers with a 'fait accompli'," a Greenpeace spokesman told journalists.

Nestle in general favours the use of genetically altered soybeans, which have been developed by Monsanto Co and are resistant to herbicides. It notes authorities in the U.S. and Europe have approved them.
But bowing to expected consumer wariness, Nestle's German subsidiary has said it will not use them in food produced in Germany.

Greenpeace activists on Friday temporarily blockaded a shipment of what they believed to be genetically altered soybeans in the Belgian Port of Antwerp, Europe's second busiest port. They had staged another protest in Hamburg.
Every week in Europe thousands of tonnes of soybeans are processed into meal and oil, which is used in a wide variety of everyday foods such as margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.
Some leading European firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever, have bowed to consumer pressure and announced they will not use the new variety even though they consider it safe.
Leading chocolate company Kraft Jacobs Suchard SA said on Friday it would not use the new soybeans in its European products for now, but was not opposed to the bean in principle on safety grounds.
